title: Leuprorelin Suppresses Angiogenesis and Malignant Progression in Endometrial Cancer via Downregulation of the ELAVL1/VEGFA Axis.
abstract: Leuprorelin, a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist, is currently used clinically to suppress estrogen-dependent endometrial cancer (EC) through pituitary desensitization. However, whether this agent exerts direct anti-neoplastic effects via post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms remains unclear. The phenotypic effects of leuprorelin were evaluated in EC cell lines using colony formation, 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) incorporation, Transwell migration, wound healing, flow cytometry, and HUVEC tube formation assays. Mechanistic exploration employed RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP), mRNA decay kinetics analysis, and RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization combined with immunofluorescence microscopy. A murine xenograft model system was implemented for in vivo validation studies. Leuprorelin treatment significantly reduced proliferation and migration of EC cells, induced apoptosis, and suppressed HUVEC tube formation. At the molecular level, leuprorelin administration reduced cytoplasmic accumulation of ELAVL1, an RNA-binding protein that physiologically associates with VEGFA transcripts and enhances their stability. This reduction resulted in accelerated decay of VEGFA mRNA and subsequent downregulation of VEGFA protein expression. Forced overexpression of VEGFA substantially abrogated the anti-tumor effects mediated by leuprorelin. In nude mouse xenograft models, leuprorelin administration suppressed tumor growth and tumor-associated neovascularization, effects that were reversed upon VEGFA overexpression. Leuprorelin impedes EC progression by disrupting ELAVL1-mediated stabilization of VEGFA mRNA, highlighting the ELAVL1/VEGFA axis as a potential therapeutic target for anti-angiogenic therapeutic intervention.

title: A pH/miR-21 dual-responsive multifunctional DNA tetrahedron for targeted tumor imaging and synergistic chemo-gene therapy.
abstract: Small interfering RNA (siRNA) presents promising prospects as a therapeutic agent; its clinical application is constrained by challenges such as inefficient delivery and off-target effects. This study developed a multifunctional DNA Tetrahedron (MDT) platform for synergistic delivery of siRNA and the chemotherapeutic agent doxorubicin (DOX) to optimize delivery efficiency and enhance therapeutic efficacy. The MDT structure incorporates aptamers for targeted cell recognition and modifies the DNA hairpins responsive to the tumor biomarker microRNA-21 (miR-21). The MDT provides degradation protection for siRNA and enables specific delivery to tumor cells. Following cellular internalization, the MDT responds to the acidic environment of lysosomes; its pH-responsive i-motif structure undergoes assembly by protonation, simultaneously reducing lysosomal acidity and inhibiting hydrolase activity, thereby facilitating protective release of siRNA. The DNA hairpins incorporated with the MDT transform structurally in response to miR-21 within tumor cells, generating a fluorescent signal and releasing DOX, thereby detecting tumor cells and initiating chemotherapy. Experimental results demonstrate that synergistic delivery of siRNA and DOX via this MDT platform significantly enhances tumor cell elimination. This study provides a universal strategy for developing intelligent therapeutic carriers; by replacing the aptamer and siRNA, the system can be customized for specific targeting and elimination of different tumor cell types.

title: Identifying phase separation modulators mediated by the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein using a structure-based drug discovery approach.
abstract: As severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) continues to evolve through mutations and acquire resistance to existing antiviral agents, the persistence of post-pandemic infections remains a significant global health concern. To address these challenges, it is crucial to develop novel therapeutic agents that target previously unexplored viral or host mechanisms. The nucleocapsid (N) protein of SARS-CoV-2 plays a critical role in viral RNA replication and genome packaging through its ability to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). Targeting the condensation of N-RNA complex could potentially serve as an effective therapeutic strategy against coronavirus infections. The present study provides a successful exemplification of antiviral agent discovery by targeting the viral N protein on the basis of its structural characteristics. A total of 23 virtual screening compounds and 16 hit derivatives were prepared. Their binding affinity and antiviral activities were evaluated using surface plasmon resonance and immunofluorescence assay, respectively. The impact of these compounds on condensate formation was verified through fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, as well as the inhibition of N condensate formation in cells. Structure-based virtual screening, target protein binding affinity quantification, and cell culture-based anti-SARS-CoV-2 assays enabled the identification a hit compound, D21. Subsequent structural optimization of series I and II yielded compound II8, which exhibits stronger binding affinity for the N protein and effectively inhibits the formation of N-RNA condensates, thereby demonstrating its potential to modulate LLPS, a mechanism underlying its antiviral activity. In vivo evaluation showed that II8 displays antiviral activity in a human ACE2-expressing mouse model when administered intranasally as a pre-incubated mixture with SARS-CoV-2. Due to the pharmacokinetic profile of compound II8, further structural modifications are still required. Our findings suggest that compound II8 may serve as a localized prophylactic nasal spray, providing valuable insights for further development of LLPS modulators as next-generation antiviral agents.

title: Weak Evolutionary Conservation of RNA-Protein Dispersion across Human and Arabidopsis Orthologs.
abstract: Gene-specific relative RNA-protein dispersion, the difference between RNA and protein variation across tissues, may be conserved over evolutionary distance if particular genes experience consistent post-transcriptional regulatory constraints. We tested this in human and Arabidopsis thaliana by comparing a scale-invariant dispersion phenotype, Bdisp, across 855 prespecified one-to-one orthologs, using tissue-resolved transcriptomic and proteomic atlases. Human and Arabidopsis Bdisp showed a weak positive association (Spearman's ρ = 0.173, P < 0.001). Adjusting for protein detectability, RNA and protein abundance, and sequence conservation reduced it to ρ = 0.068 (bootstrap 95% confidence interval [CI] - 0.0003 to 0.136), although its direction was stable across four prespecified cohorts (ρ = 0.063-0.088). Masking 89 orthologs in four prespecified ancient systems (ribosome, proteasome, chaperone complexes and respiratory chain) lowered the adjusted association (Δρ = - 0.019, 95% CI -0.038 to -0.001) but did not change two alternative RNA-protein metrics. Exploratory analyses added after the primary analysis showed that this reduction was no larger than that from removing 89 random orthologs (two-sided P = 0.11) and was attributable to the respiratory-chain complex alone (24 pairs; Δρ = - 0.022; P = 0.00025). Among 447 sufficiently represented Gene Ontology (GO) terms, 119 unadjusted correlations, but no covariate-adjusted correlations, passed Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Genome-wide conservation of RNA-protein dispersion between human and Arabidopsis is therefore weak once abundance and detectability are considered, the residual signal is not localized to ancient core systems as a class, and the data do not identify a mode of natural selection.

title: The SlHYL1-SlRBP1 module integrates gibberellin metabolism to promote plant height in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum).
abstract: Plant height is an essential agronomic trait that significantly influences crop yield and quality. The HYPONASTIC LEAVES 1 (HYL1), a core component of microRNA biogenesis, remains poorly understood in terms of its regulatory mechanisms on agronomic traits in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Sl). In this study, we demonstrated that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of SlHYL1 caused dwarfism, and partial suppression of SlHYL1 in tomato cultivar "Ailsa Craig" (AC) via RNA interference (RNAi) increased internode number but reduced internode length, resulting in a semi-dwarf phenotype, confirming the role of SlHYL1 in regulating plant height. Cytological analysis showed that SlHYL1 suppression decreased both cell number and size within internodes. Yeast two-hybrid screening identified that SlHYL1 interacted with another tomato RNA-binding protein 1 (SlRBP1). Knockdown of SlRBP1 resembled the SlHYL1-RNAi semi-dwarf phenotype. Further studies revealed that the SlHYL1-SlRBP1 module additively promotes the expression of gibberellin (GA) biosynthetic genes, thereby facilitating GA accumulation. Additionally, the dwarf phenotypes of both SlHYL1-RNAi and SlRBP1-RNAi plants were partially rescued by exogenous GA3 application. Notably, unlike SlHYL1, SlRBP1 did not affect the biogenesis of most miRNAs. In summary, our findings demonstrate that the SlHYL1-SlRBP1 module regulates tomato plant height by enhancing GA accumulation.

title: Gas-phase stabilization by tertiary interactions in yeast tRNAPhe and quaternary contacts in a small RNA-RNA complex.
abstract: Native mass spectrometry (nMS) and ion mobility (IM) are now established tools for the structural analysis of proteins and protein complexes, but their application to RNAs and RNA-RNA assemblies remains less developed. Here, we examine how magnesium, ionization polarity, solution temperature, and collisional activation influence the mass-corrected collision cross section (mCCS) of wild-type (WT) and a structurally destabilized mutant (MT) yeast tRNAPhe. Under positive-polarity ionization, magnesium was essential for WT tRNAPhe to fold into and retain native-like structures. In 2 mM magnesium acetate, increasing the solution temperature from 25 to 60°C produced little change in the mCCS of WT tRNAPhe, whereas the mCCS of MT tRNAPhe increased. Collisional activation further distinguished the two constructs: increasing the trap collision energy induced a pronounced decrease in the mCCS of WT but only a modest decrease for MT tRNAPhe, consistent with the absence of magnesium-supported tertiary contacts in the mutant. We also assessed the HJ3 RNA-RNA heterodimer using collision- and surface-induced dissociation (CID and SID, respectively). CID primarily resulted in charge stripping, while SID generated proportionally charged monomers, indicating preservation of native quaternary contacts. Collectively, these results demonstrate how IM-nMS measurements can be leveraged to gain insights into the tertiary and quaternary RNA structures and their gas-phase stability.

title: Queuosine-modification dependent histidyl tRNA fragment promotes cell-type dependent proliferation.
abstract: tRNA fragments (tRFs) are natural, small non-coding RNAs produced by endogenous ribonucleolytic cleavage of tRNAs. tRFs play a role in many biological pathways, including regulation of cell proliferation. Specific tRNA modifications affect tRF biogenesis. Queuosine (Q) modification occurs at the wobble anticodon nucleotide of 4 mammalian tRNAs and protects these tRNAs from fragmentation. Here, we investigated cell-type and tRNA Q-modification dependencies on mammalian cell proliferation. We found that Q-modified tRNA can either increase, decrease, or make no difference in proliferation. Proliferation decreased in MCF7, a breast cancer cell line, when tRNAs were Q-modified and dependent on the modification enzyme complex, QTRT1/2. MCF7 proliferation increases upon the transfection of Q-modification-dependent tRFHis or decreases upon knockdown of endogenous tRFHis. Consistent with Q-dependent proliferation reduction, polysome profiling showed decreased translation efficiency of ribosomal proteins. Finally, protein pull-down of MCF7 lysates using tRFHis identified Musashi RNA-binding protein 2 (Msi2) as a tRFHis-binding protein. Msi2 knockdown reduced the Q-modification-dependent or tRFHis dependent cell proliferation effect. Our results illustrate a highly cell-type-dependent proliferation effect of tRNA Q-modification, suggesting multi-faceted mechanisms in studying this ubiquitous tRNA modification.

title: Structure-based virtual screening and molecular dynamics reveal saquinavir as a potential inhibitor of the Bhanja virus nucleoprotein.
abstract: Tick-borne diseases caused by the Bhanja virus (BHAV) have recently emerged as a significant threat to both human and livestock health. Currently, there are no approved antiviral agents available to control BHAV infection, highlighting the urgent need to identify potential therapeutic targets and effective drugs. Since nucleoprotein is a key structural and functional component essential for the replication and assembly of RNA viruses, we hypothesized that inhibition of the BHAV nucleoprotein could suppress viral growth and replication. In this study, we employed a structure-based drug repurposing approach to identify existing antiviral compounds capable of targeting the BHAV nucleoprotein. The three-dimensional structure of the BHAV nucleoprotein was modeled and subjected to molecular docking with 50 known antiviral drugs. Among them, saquinavir demonstrated the highest binding affinity and most favorable interaction profile. To further evaluate the thermodynamic stability of the nucleoprotein-saquinavir complex, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed for 150 ns in triplicate. The simulation analyses confirmed the structural stability and sustained interaction of saquinavir with the BHAV nucleoprotein over time. Overall, our findings suggest that saquinavir may serve as a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for the inhibition of BHAV replication, offering a potential strategy for the control of tick-borne viral diseases.

title: Genome-Wide Analysis of Protein Binding to DNA in Plastids by ptChIP-seq.
abstract: Plastids contain their own genomes encoding essential components of the photosynthetic apparatus and gene expression machinery. Transcription in plastids is mediated by two RNA polymerases, nuclear-encoded (NEP) and plastid-encoded RNA polymerase (PEP). Transcription, together with the binding of nuclear-encoded plastid nucleoid-associated proteins and dynamic tethering of nucleoids to plastid membranes, shapes nucleoid organization and function. Understanding these processes is critical for deciphering the regulation of gene expression in these organelles, which underpins chloroplast biogenesis, photosynthesis, and plant development. Here we present an optimized procedure for genome-wide detection of protein-binding sites in vivo using plastid chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled with high-throughput sequencing (ptChIP-seq). Compared with standard ChIP-seq protocols, this method employs a high formaldehyde concentration for cross-linking that maximizes DNA recovery without detectable nonspecific binding when proper controls are used. We use a custom Illumina-compatible library preparation incorporating multiplexing strategies that enables pooling of many libraries per experiment, reducing per-sample costs. Detailed procedures are provided for Arabidopsis thaliana at two developmental stages, but the method can be adapted to other species with appropriate modifications to chloroplast enrichment. Although we focus on detection of PEP, these protocols are applicable to detection of other endogenous and epitope-tagged plastid proteins that directly interact with DNA. Unlike approaches relying on chloroplast ChIP-qPCR or low-resolution ChIP-chip, ptChIP-seq generates cost-effective high-resolution genome-wide maps of binding sites of any DNA-associated protein of interest in the plastid. This enables comprehensive investigation of active DNA metabolic processes within plastids, including transcription, replication, and DNA repair, and opens up avenues for exploring the dynamic interplay between nucleoid architecture, membrane association, and gene expression in response to developmental and environmental cues. © 2026 The Author(s). Basic Protocol 1: Plant material collection, chloroplast enrichment, and cross-linking Alternate Protocol 1: Working with young seedlings Basic Protocol 2: Immunoprecipitation and reverse cross-linking Basic Protocol 3: DNA isolation, ptChIP validation, library preparation, and sequencing Basic Protocol 4: Data analysis.

title: The intergenerational and transgenerational effects of miRNAs in fertility, obesity and stress responses.
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators that play pivotal roles in diverse physiological and pathological processes. They primarily act by inhibiting protein translation and promoting degradation of messenger RNA (mRNA), thereby inducing post-transcriptional regulatory effects. Most miRNAs can travel through blood, in extracellular vesicles, and between maternal and fetal tissues. When altered miRNAs were present in germ cells, this induces epigenetic inheritance, which influences embryonic development after fertilization. Aberrant miRNA expression is associated with a wide range of human diseases. This review article will summarize current evidence on how miRNA dysregulation contributes to transgenerational effects on reproduction, metabolism, and stress-related phenotypes. This research focuses on the impacts of miRNAs on reproductive impairment, obesity, and stress-related phenotypes, and highlights evidence that these epigenetic changes can persist across multiple generations. Relevant studies were identified mainly through PubMed database using "miRNA" and "transgenerational effect", with a third keyword according to the topic of interest, including "reproduction", "hormones", "spermatogenesis", "obesity", "high-fat diet", "diabetes", "stress", and "therapy". In reproduction, environmental pollutants (including endocrine disruptors) can alter miRNA expression, impairing gonadal development, reducing primordial germ cells, inducing granulosa cell apoptosis, and disrupting sex hormone synthesis. miRNA-dependent pathways also affect spermatogenesis, sperm function, and oocyte development. In obesity, miRNAs regulate adipogenesis by modulating signaling pathways and transcription programs that control fat-cell formation. Paternal high-fat diet and gestational diabetes can shift miRNA profiles, raising offspring risk for obesity and metabolic disease. Chronic stress changes miRNA expression in germ cells and embryos, shaping stress reactivity and social behavior in later generations. Prenatal maternal stress is linked to lasting psychiatric vulnerability in offspring, with effects potentially persisting across multiple generations without continued stress. Overall, miRNA dysregulation can impair reproduction, metabolism, and stress responses, and these effects may be transmitted transgenerationally via epigenetic mechanisms.

title: Multi-Omics Profiling of Cigarette Smoke-Associated Changes in Cell Models of Human Liver, Intestine and Lung.
abstract: Cigarette smoke is a complex mixture that affects toxicological and pharmacological mechanisms in multiple organs, including liver, intestine, and lung. Therefore, an integrated multi-omics approach was applied to characterize cigarette smoke extract (CSE)-induced effects across human in vitro models of liver, intestine and lung. Primary human hepatocytes, biopsy-derived intestinal organoids, alveolar A549 cells, primary bronchial and small airway epithelial cells were exposed to CSE and analyzed using RNA sequencing and untargeted proteomics. Across tissues and omics-layers, activation of aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) signaling and strong induction of CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 was identified as cross-tissue response. CYP1A1 was the only overlapping molecule among deregulated proteins across all in vitro models. Consistent deregulation of G protein-coupled receptor-signaling was observed. Overall, tissue-specific adaptations were identified. Liver models showed upregulation of xenobiotic and metabolic pathways, intestine models displayed downregulation of cell cycle processes consistent with growth arrest. Lung models should be considered cautiously because of heterogeneity between cell models but demonstrated a shared response of CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 deregulation. Cross-omics comparisons of RNA sequencing and proteomics data revealed moderate correlations (ρ = 0.43-0.64) and limited overlap of individual molecules, highlighting the importance of post-transcriptional regulation. Network and upstream regulator analyses predicted a coordinated stress response accompanied by modulation of inflammatory signaling. These findings demonstrate that cigarette smoke induces shared pathway-level responses, alongside tissue-specific adaptations. This underscores the importance of considering multiple organ systems in toxicological and pharmacological assessments. This comprehensive dataset provides a resource that may support further hypothesis-driven analysis of cigarette smoke-related mechanisms.

title: Schizophrenia Multitarget Therapy: Rapamycin Coordinates PI3K-AKT/mTOR Signaling with Cytokine Networks.
abstract: Rapamycin (RAPA) is an inhibitor of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) that may modulate neuropsychiatric conditions. The global prevalence of psychiatric disorders is increasing due to growing socioeconomic stressors. Despite the promising therapeutic indications of RAPA, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying the effects of RAPA on schizophrenia are unclear. This study investigates anti-schizophrenia mechanisms of RAPA using network pharmacology and molecular docking. Potential pharmacological targets of RAPA were identified by searching the SwissTargetPrediction, GeneCards, and Similarity Ensemble Approach databases. Schizophrenia-related targets were identified by searching GeneCards and Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man. Bioinformatics analysis (including analyses of protein-protein interaction networks and enrichment analyses) was conducted to identify core targets and signaling pathways. Molecular docking simulations were conducted to assess drug binding affinities to core targets. Cross-referencing 4013 targets linked to schizophrenic pathology with 1954 RAPA-associated targets yielded 749 shared targets. Protein-protein interaction network analysis revealed the following core targets: interleukin-6 (IL-6), interferon-gamma, IL-10, IL-4, IL-2, IL-1 beta (IL-1B), tumor necrosis factor, IL-5, IL-17A, and IL-1A. Functional enrichment assessments revealed that signal transduction, positive regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II, positive regulation of gene expression, and positive regulation of DNA-templated transcription are critical biological processes involved in RAPA antipsychotic effects. Pathway analysis revealed that the PI3K-AKT signaling cascade is a central mechanism mediating the effects of RAPA. Molecular docking simulations confirmed strong binding affinities between RAPA and the core targets. Rapamycin may modulate cytokine networks and PI3K-AKT/mTOR signaling pathways implicated in schizophrenia. These in-silico findings are hypothesis-generating and require experimental and clinical validation.

title: Epigallocatechin-3-gallate attenuates PAR-2-mediated inflammatory signaling and preserves markers of mitochondrial integrity in osteoarthritic chondrocytes.
abstract: Epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), the principal catechin of green tea, exhibits broad anti-inflammatory properties; however, its effect on protease-activated receptor-2 (PAR-2)-mediated signaling in osteoarthritis (OA) has not been investigated. Here, we report that EGCG (5-10 µM) dose-dependently suppresses PAR-2 expression at both mRNA and protein levels in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated human chondrocytes derived from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. This upstream inhibition attenuated ERK1/2 phosphorylation (pERK/total ERK ratio reduced below basal levels at 10 µM) and produced concordant suppression of three functionally linked effector arms: (i) pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, MCP-1), with near-maximal inhibition at 10 µM and a saturation plateau at 20 µM; (ii) the SOX4-ADAMTS-5 catabolic axis (81.9% and 66.2% protein reduction, respectively); and (iii) RANK/RANKL surface expression. EGCG also restored mitochondrial membrane potential and biomass to near-homeostatic levels. Crucially, small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated PAR-2 silencing reduced LPS-induced TNF-α by ~38% and substantially blunted EGCG's incremental efficacy, supporting PAR-2 as a predominant, though not exclusive, mediator of EGCG's anti-inflammatory action. The effective concentrations employed are physiologically attainable through dietary green tea consumption, as documented by a comprehensive survey of EGCG content across 36 commercial varieties. These findings support PAR-2 as a candidate upstream target of EGCG in OA chondrocytes and suggest a mechanistic model involving PAR-2 → ERK1/2 → TNF-α/SOX4/ADAMTS-5, through which a dietary polyphenol exerts coordinated anti-inflammatory and anti-catabolic effects, while preserving structural and thermodynamic markers of mitochondrial integrity.

title: Erlotinib in a once-daily high-dose oral regimen could mitigate Chikungunya virus titer in mice.
abstract: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is a re-emerging arbovirus that causes debilitating inflammatory arthritis, for which no approved antiviral therapy currently exists. This study investigated the potential of repurposing erlotinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, as an anti-CHIKV agent. Erlotinib demonstrated promising in vitro antiviral activity, with EC50 values in the low micromolar range and a favorable selectivity index. However, in vivo evaluation in C57BL/6 mice revealed pharmacokinetic limitations, characterized by rapid absorption and clearance, resulting in insufficient drug exposure under standard dosing regimens. Escalation to an intensive four-times-daily (QID) regimen successfully maintained plasma concentrations above the in vitro therapeutic threshold but led to significant body weight loss and failed to reduce viral titers or viral RNA levels in infected tissues. However, a once-daily (OD) regimen improved tolerability and significantly reduced footpad and serum viral titers relative to vehicle-treated controls. Notably, despite the lack of virological control in the QID regimen, erlotinib treatment reduced leukocyte infiltration and tissue inflammation in both treatment regimens, indicating a host-directed immunomodulatory effect. Overall, these findings highlight the critical role of dosing frequency in determining erlotinib's in vivo antiviral efficacy against CHIKV and suggest that once-daily (OD) administration may represent a more viable dosing strategy for further evaluation of erlotinib as a host-directed antiviral against CHIKV. Future strategies should also explore combination approaches with direct-acting antivirals to achieve more viral suppression and mitigation of disease pathology, as well as Structure-Activity Relationship (SAR)-guided scaffold optimization to improve in vivo pharmacokinetic profiles.

title: Palmitoylation-related gene signature analysis links ENPP6 to potential protection of renal tubule against ischemia-reperfusion injury.
abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI), particularly ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), lacks effective targeted therapies. Protein S-palmitoylation is a reversible lipid modification involved in cellular stress responses, but its role in AKI remains unclear. We aimed to identify palmitoylation-related genes in AKI and explore their potential functions. Public transcriptome datasets of AKI kidney tissues were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Palmitoylation-related common hub genes were screened by integrating DEG analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data and online clinical databases were used to determine cellular localization and clinical relevance. ENPP6 was further validated in a mouse renal IRI model and hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R)-treated renal tubule cells. Six candidate common hub genes were identified: EDN1, VMP1, ENPP6, MYC, CXCR4, and EFNA1. Among them, ENPP6 was enriched in renal tubular cells and showed the strongest association with indices of renal function. ENPP6 expression was significantly reduced in the renal tubules of IRI mice at both the mRNA and protein levels. In renal tubule cells, ENPP6 overexpression was accompanied by increased overall protein S-palmitoylation. Functionally, ENPP6 overexpression improved cell viability and alleviated H/R-induced injury. ENPP6 expression was reduced in renal IRI and was positively associated with renal function. In renal tubular cells, ENPP6 overexpression was accompanied by increased global protein S-palmitoylation and reduced H/R-induced injury. These findings identify ENPP6 as a potential protective factor and a candidate for further mechanistic investigation in ischemic AKI.

title: Protective effect of gossypin against high-fat diet-induced atherosclerosis in rats: Role of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase/AKT/mechanistic target of rapamycin pathway and gut microbiota.
abstract: Over the last decade, there has been a global prevalence of high morbidity and mortality associated with atherosclerotic disease. Gossypin exhibits the anti-inflammatory and protective effect against various disease. The current protocol demonstrated the antiatherosclerotic effect of gossypin against high-fat diet (HFD)-induced atherosclerosis (AS) in rats and explored the underlying mechanism. HFD and Vitamin D3 (600,000 IU/kg) were used to induce AS in rats, and the rats were treated with different doses of gossypin and rosuvastatin, respectively. Body weight, organ weights, inflammatory, cardiac, and lipid parameters, as well as micro-RNA (mRNA) expression, were estimated. The rat faces were collected for the determination of gut microbiota. Gossypin treatment markedly reduced body weight and altered organ weights. Gossypin treatment Remarkably modulated the level of cardiac parameters such as creatine kinase (CK), CK myocardial band, lactate dehydrogenase, cardiac troponin I, thromboxane B2, endothelin-1; lipid parameters such as total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), high density lipoprotein (HDL), low density lipoprotein (LDL), very LDL, TC/HDL, TG/HDL, free fatty acid; hepatic parameters, namely, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase; inflammatory parameters such as cyclooxygenase-2, inducible nitric oxide synthetase, C-reactive protein, prostaglandin E2, nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB); inflammatory cytokines include interleukin (IL)-1β, 6, 5, 10, 17, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), C-X-C Motif chemokine ligand 1 (CXCL1), respectively. Gossypin treatment also altered the mRNA expression of intercellular adhesion molecule-1, vascular cell adhesion molecule-1, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA-1), liver X receptor-α, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ, toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3, NF-κBp65, myeloid differentiation primary response 88, IL-1 β, IL-6, IL-17, TNF-α, phosphorylated AMP-activated protein kinase, phosphorylated mechanistic target of rapamycin (p-mTOR), phosphorylated phosphoinositide 3-kinase (p-PI3K), and phosphorylated protein kinase B (p-AKT), respectively. Gossypin treatment remarkably modulated the abundance of Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, F/B ratio, deferribacteraceae and cyanobacteria. Gossypin exhibited the anti-AS effect through alteration of PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway and gut microbiota.

title: A single liver-sparing myotropic AAV ameliorates muscular dystrophy in humanized mice by base editing.
abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is caused by mutations in the DMD gene, most of which are large exon deletions that result in loss of dystrophin protein. Adenine base editing (ABE) enables permanent gene correction by modifying splice sites to cause exon skipping and restoration of the DMD open reading frame. We previously demonstrated that adeno-associated virus 9-mediated (AAV9-mediated) delivery of adenine base editors allows efficient gene editing in mouse models of DMD. However, conventional AAV-based gene delivery approaches are complicated by their limited packaging capacity and high-dose-related toxicity. Here, we describe a single AAV vector encoding a compact adenine base editor, SlugABE8e, and a single-guide RNA, which enable efficient editing in a humanized DMD mouse model at a lower dose using the muscle-tropic MyoAAV4 capsid. Systemic MyoAAV4A delivery in juvenile DMD mice efficiently restored dystrophin expression in the heart and skeletal muscles. This molecular rescue was accompanied by reduced serum creatine kinase activity and diminished muscle pathology. A liver-detargeted MyoAAV4E-off capsid eliminated viral entry and editing in the liver. We also explored a high-fidelity base editor, SlugHF-ABE8e(V106W), which showed similar on-target and off-target editing to SlugABE8e. Together, these findings establish an all-in-one AAV strategy that efficiently mitigates DMD disease progression.

title: Comparative Analysis of Exonic SSR-Containing Genes in Three Diving Duck Species Reveals Shared Functional Themes.
abstract: Simple sequence repeats (SSRs) are ubiquitous components of eukaryotic genomes that contribute to genome evolution, genetic variation, and gene regulation. Although genome-wide SSR landscapes have been extensively characterized across vertebrates, the cross-species distribution and functional associations of exonic SSR-containing genes remain poorly understood, particularly in non-model birds. To address this knowledge gap, we performed a comparative analysis of chromosome-level genome assemblies from three diving duck species (Aythya ferina, Aythya marila, and Netta rufina) to investigate genome-wide SSR patterns and the cross-species sharing and functional characteristics of exonic SSR-containing genes. Comparative analyses of genome-wide SSRs revealed pronounced interspecific variation in SSR abundance and repeat composition, whereas exonic SSR abundance showed more similar values after normalization by total annotated exon sequence length. Cross-species comparison identified 4336 exonic SSR-containing genes shared among all three species, greatly outnumbering the species-specific gene sets. Functional enrichment analyses identified four broad functional themes associated with these shared genes: (i) gene transcription and epigenetic regulation, (ii) protein homeostasis and the ubiquitin-proteasome system, (iii) development, differentiation and morphogenesis, and (iv) stress response and cellular maintenance. The most significantly enriched categories were associated with transcriptional regulation, chromatin remodeling, RNA processing, and epigenetic regulation, whereas autophagy- and other cellular-maintenance pathways indicated additional associations with stress-response processes. These functional associations should be interpreted cautiously because they may be influenced by cross-species annotation limitations and gene-architecture differences. Collectively, our results reveal distinct patterns for genome-wide and exonic SSRs distribution among the three diving duck species and identify shared functional associations of genes containing exonic SSRs. These findings provide a comparative genomic framework for future investigations of exonic SSRs in waterfowl and other non-model vertebrates.

title: Kinesin motor proteins as host factors regulating viral infection: Mechanisms of exploitation, emerging paradigms, and therapeutic horizons.
abstract: Intracellular transport via microtubules is integral to eukaryotic cell function, and viruses have developed intricate mechanisms to exploit this system at nearly every stage of their replication cycle. The mammalian kinesin superfamily, consisting of 14 distinct families, enables anterograde transport that is used by both DNA and RNA viruses. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of how a wide range of viral pathogens-including herpesviruses, human immunodeficiency virus type 1, vaccinia virus, hepatitis B virus (HBV), influenza virus, and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-interact with specific kinesin family members to promote viral entry, genome trafficking, organization of replication compartments, assembly, and egress. Recent findings underscore the role of the kinesin-4 family member KIF4A as a novel host factor for HBV. The therapeutic potential of modulating the surface expression of the HBV-entry receptor (NTCP) is discussed, either by suppressing KIF4 expression-necessary for anti-retrograde transport of NTCP to the cell surface-or by disrupting the NTCP-KIF4 interaction. Additionally, emerging pharmacological approaches targeting kinesin-dependent transport are evaluated. By establishing a unified framework that connects motor protein biology to virology, this review identifies key knowledge gaps and outlines future research directions for the development of broad-spectrum, host-targeted, antiviral therapies.

title: A Hepatitis B virus pregenomic RNA based minigene transcript utilizes polypyrimidine tract binding protein regulated NXF1-NXT1 nuclear export pathway.
abstract: Hepatitis B virus, a pararetrovirus and member of hepadnaviridae family, harbours a partially double-stranded DNA genome that is transcribed by the host RNA polymerase II to generate an intron-containing pregenomic RNA (pgRNA). Nuclear export of pgRNA utilizing the canonical host pathways remains central to successful virus replication since it is reverse transcribed by the viral P protein within the nucleocapsid in cytoplasm. We provide direct microscopic evidence of Polypyrimidine tract binding protein (PTB) mediated inhibition of nuclear export of a pgRNA based intron-containing pre-mRNA (CPS-PRE) with quantitative RNA-FISH. We also demonstrate through RNA immunoprecipitation experiments that CPS-PRE minigene transcripts stably interact with members of NXF1-NXT1 pathway and no crosslinking with karyopherin CRM1 could be seen. Our data reinforces a novel aspect of PTB in pre-mRNA nuclear export for active retention of intron-containing transcripts and directly shows the ability of pgRNA components to interact with NXF1-NXT1 heterodimer.

title: Isothermal based rapid and direct detection of bean common mosaic virus (BCMV) from crude plant sap.
abstract: Bean common mosaic virus (BCMV) is a serious viral pathogen of leguminous crops especially common beans. BCMV is transmitted through infected seeds and can also spread horizontally by aphid vectors in a non-persistent manner. It is highly stable within the embryo of seed that is the major factor contributing for its long-distance dissemination across continents. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop a reliable, rapid and cost-effective diagnostic method that can facilitate the detection of the virus in seed certification programs and plant quarantine facilities, thereby prevents its further spread. The present study describes an efficient and accurate detection of BCMV by reverse transcriptase-recombinase polymerase amplification (RT-RPA) assay. The primers were designed from highly conserved region of coat protein region. The BCMV-specific primers successfully amplified fragment of the coat protein (CP) gene under isothermal conditions at 37 °C within 20 min. The limit of detection of the developed assay was determined using both purified RNA and crude plant sap extract. In both cases, the assay exhibited higher sensitivity than conventional RT-PCR, enabling the detection of BCMV at lower template concentrations. In addition, specificity of the assay was tested by cross reaction with closely related non-target viruses (bean common mosaic necrosis virus (BCMNV), clover yellow vein virus (ClYVV), soybean mosaic virus (SMV) and cucumber mosaic virus (CMV) BCMNV). The RT-RPA assay accurately distinguished BCMV from other non-target viruses showing comparable specificity with RT-PCR. To enhance the suitability of the assay for resource-limited settings and reduce the overall detection time, the assay was adapted to accurately detect BCMV directly from crude sap. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13337-026-00985-7.

title: Endothelial-specific Tie2 knockout mouse model - Tie2fl/fl;Cdh5-creERT2(+/-): a potent tool for inducible Tie2 deletion in vasculature across multiple organs.
abstract: TEK receptor tyrosine kinase (Tie2) is predominantly expressed on endothelial cells and is known to play a critical role in vascular development and stability. Due to its role in vascular development, germline knockout of Tie2 is embryonically lethal. In this study we aimed to generate an inducible Tie2 knockout mouse model that specifically targets the mature endothelium. Mice with floxed Tie2 exon 9 alleles (Tie2fl/fl) were crossed with heterozygous Cdh5-creERT2(+/-) mice to generate Tie2fl/fl;Cdh5-creERT2(+/-) (cTie2-KO) mice. Deletion of Tie2 in the endothelium of adult cTie2-KO mice was induced by intraperitoneal injection of tamoxifen, where Tie2fl/fl/Cre- (Tie2fl/fl) mice served as controls. Five weeks after the start of treatment, organs were evaluated for Tie2 deletion at the DNA, RNA, and protein level. Another set of organs were collected for immunocytochemical analysis, to visually assess the expression levels of Tie2 within the tissue vasculature. The functional effect of the loss of Tie2 on the vasculature was evaluated by measuring vascular permeability in all organs in a separate set of mice. Tie2 exon 9 was deleted at the DNA level in the brains of cTie2-KO mice. All organs in cTie2-KO mice showed a significant reduction in expression of Tie2 mRNA at multiple exon levels as compared to Tie2fl/fl controls. Total protein evaluation via ELISA showed a significant reduction of Tie2 in all tissue homogenates of cTie2-KO mice. Co-localization of Tie2 with a pan-endothelial marker demonstrated that Tie2 expression was lost in the microvascular segments of all organs evaluated, as compared to control mice. Notably, vascular permeability as measured by dextran extravasation was increased in the brain parenchyma of cTie2-KO mice as compared to control mice. Deletion of Tie2 did not affect peripheral organ permeability. We have successfully generated a Tie2 conditional knockout mouse with significant endothelial specific deletion across multiple organs. Furthermore, at baseline we see functional deficits in cTie2-KO mice that are related specifically to blood brain barrier permeability independent of permeability in peripheral organs. This mouse model holds promise for opportunities to investigate the role of Tie2 in multiple organ vasculatures in health and disease conditions.

title: Complete mitogenome assembly of Lilium amoenum E. H. Wilson ex Sealy revealed its multiple chromosomal configurations, genome evolution, phylogenetic implications, and RNA-editing.
abstract: Lilium amoenum E. H. Wilson ex Sealy is a wild lily species endemic to Yunnan, China, and is of considerable ornamental and scientific interest owing to its solitary, pendulous, fragrant, rose-purple flowers. Although the chloroplast genome of this species has been reported, its mitogenome has not yet been characterized. To address this gap, we employed a hybrid sequencing strategy combining Illumina short-read and Nanopore long-read data to assemble and annotate, for the first time, the complete mitogenome of L. amoenum. The mitogenome of L. amoenum exhibits a distinctive multichromosomal architecture comprising 13 circular chromosomes and one linear chromosome, with a total length of 789,335 bp and an overall GC content of 45.11%. In total, 55 genes were annotated, including 37 protein-coding genes (PCGs), 3 rRNA genes, and 15 tRNA genes. We also identified 171 simple sequence repeats (SSRs), eight tandem repeats, and 509 dispersed repeats. Homology analysis detected 14 plastid-derived fragments totaling 4,723 bp, representing 0.60% of the mitogenome. Collinearity analysis revealed extensive genomic rearrangements between L. amoenum and its close relatives, indicating substantial structural divergence during mitogenome evolution. Phylogenetic analysis based on the mitogenomes of 26 species showed that L. amoenum clusters with other members of Lilium, consistent with the APG IV classification system. In addition, 493 C-to-U RNA editing sites in the coding regions of mitochondrial PCGs were predicted. Lastly, we successfully validated five randomly selected RNA editing sites. This study provides the first complete mitogenome of L. amoenum, revealing its unique multi-chromosomal configuration. Moreover, it offers a valuable genomic resource for breeding, species identification, germplasm conservation, and phylogenetic studies within Lilium species.

title: Synthetic lethal screens reveal p300/CBP as a vulnerability for GNAQ-driven uveal melanomas.
abstract: Uveal melanoma is the most common intraocular cancer in adults, driven by activating mutations in GNAQ or GNA11, which encode the G proteins Gαq and Gα11. Currently, therapeutic options for uveal melanoma, particularly metastatic uveal melanoma, remain limited. Through an isogenic CRISPR screening approach, we identify EP300, which encodes the protein lysine acetyltransferase p300, as a top synthetic lethal vulnerability in the context of GNAQ mutation. Notably, CREBBP, which encodes the closely related paralogue CBP, also emerges among the top-ranked candidates. Mechanistically, we find that p300 and CBP support YAP-dependent transcription downstream of oncogenic Gαq in uveal melanoma through interactions with YAP at chromatin. These interactions enhance H3K27 acetylation at the promoters and putative enhancers of YAP target genes and promote the recruitment of RNA polymerase II and CDK9. Using multiple in vivo models representing clinically relevant stages of Gαq-mutant uveal melanoma, we find that p300 inhibition, by both genetic and pharmacological approaches, profoundly impairs tumor growth and metastasis. Taken together, this study establishes p300 as a potential therapeutic target for Gαq-driven uveal melanoma, which is dependent on unrestrained YAP signaling.

title: Expression and purification of SP6 RNA polymerase for in vitro transcription.
abstract: Construction of a plasmid for efficient overexpression of SP6 RNA polymerase in E. coli and method of purification of multi-milligram quantities of this enzyme by two chromatographic steps is described. SP6 RNA polymerase purified by this method is highly active and stable in described storage conditions at -20 °C for many years. Due to its specific 5' sequence (5'-GAATACA…) uncapped mRNA synthesized by SP6 RNA polymerase can be used for cell-free translation yielding several times more protein product than uncapped mRNAs produced by other polymerases. These factors greatly reduce the costs of in vitro production of mRNA for cell-free translation, improving the feasibility of this protein expression system for various applications.

title: Yeast protein-derived methionine alleviates ethanol-induced acute gastric mucosal injury by targeting TNF-α/NOS2 and modulating the NOD-like receptor signaling pathway.
abstract: Ethanol directly stimulates and damages the gastric mucosa, leading to impairment of the mucus-bicarbonate barrier and mechanical barrier, which is the primary factor of gastric ulcer formation. Yeast protein (YP), an emerging microbial food ingredient, has shown potential in mucosal protection. However, its bioactive components and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study aims to evaluate the protective effect of YP hydrolyzed by papanin (YP-P) against ethanol-induced acute gastric mucosal injury, identify the key bioactive compound, and elucidate the molecular mechanism by which it alleviates gastric mucosal damage. In this study, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), immunofluorescence (IF), western blotting (WB), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and other experimental techniques were used to evaluate the protective effects of YP-P by establishing ethanol-induced gastric mucosal injury models in vitro and in vivo. RNA sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, peptidomics, virtual screening, molecular docking, network pharmacology, proteomics, and multi-omics analysis techniques were used to determine the potential targets and molecular mechanisms of YP-P in alleviating gastric mucosal damage. Finally, the inhibition of bioactive compounds identified in YP on the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD)-like receptor signaling pathway was verified through cell experiments. The protective effects of papain-hydrolyzed YP (YP-P) were demonstrated by establishing ethanol-induced gastric mucosal injury models in vitro and in vivo. Fractionation via centrifugation and ultrafiltration identified the component with molecular weight less than 5 kDa (YP-P < 5 kDa) as the primary protective fraction. Integrating multi-omics with virtual screening and network pharmacology, methionine (Met) was identified as the key bioactive compound within YP-P < 5 kDa. Mechanism studies revealed that Met alleviates ethanol-induced acute gastric mucosal injury by targeting tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)/inducible nitrogen oxide synthase (NOS2) and modulating the NOD-like receptor signaling pathway. These findings highlight the protective effect of YP and its bioactive compound in the prevention and management of gastric mucosal injury, providing reference for their application as gastric mucosal protectants in functional ingredient.

title: Age-related changes in the transcriptional profile associated with albumen biosynthesis in the magnum of broiler breeder hens.
abstract: Broiler chicken production is critical for meeting the growing global demand for affordable protein. However, intensive selection for rapid growth and feed efficiency has led to hyperphagia and obesity in broiler breeder hens, negatively affecting egg production, egg quality, and hatchability. Egg albumen, produced in the magnum, is essential for embryonic development and early chick growth. This study aims to identify the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and biological pathways involved in albumen biosynthesis in the magnum (comparing young vs aged hens). The magnum tissues were collected from broiler breeder hens at peak production, designated as the young group (35 weeks, n = 30), and from those in declined production, designated as the aged group (50 weeks, n = 30). Total RNA was isolated and subjected to RNA sequencing (n = 5/group). The significantly upregulated genes with putative roles in egg albumen biosynthesis were confirmed by quantitative PCR. In the magnum, a total of 75 genes were upregulated, while 52 were downregulated. The most highly upregulated and downregulated genes were categorized based on their putative functions: egg white synthesis (AMDHD1, FER, CTNNA3), molecular communication (VAPA, PIP5K1B), oviduct regeneration (ADAM19, CFAP100, AMD1, TM4SF19, SLC39A13, VMO1), and defense (ZBTB46, STAM2, OVoDA3). Post-translational protein phosphorylation was the most significantly enriched Reactome pathway, involving the genes DNAJC3, PPP3CA, TF, SPARCL1, PDIA6, SGPP2, HSP90B1, and PNPLA2. The study identified DEGs, genetic networks, and pathways that can serve as genetic markers for selecting high-quality egg-producing broiler breeder hens.

title: The HSV-1 US1 gene product targets the histone chaperone ASF1 to suppress H3K9 acetylation.
abstract: It is commonly known that the Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) manipulates host gene expression to facilitate its reproduction. HSV-1 regulates host and viral transcription through coordinated effects on transcription factors, RNA polymerase II, transcription initiation and elongation, and host chromatin dynamics. However, how HSV-1 proteins regulate host histone chaperones and histone modifications remains incompletely understood. Here, we identified a functional relationship between the HSV-1 immediate-early protein ICP22 and anti-silencing function 1 (ASF1), a histone chaperone with two human isoforms, ASF1a and ASF1b. ICP22 associated with both ASF1 isoforms in transfected and HSV-1-infected cells. Compared with wild-type HSV-1 infection, deletion of ICP22 largely restored ASF1 transcript and protein levels and attenuated the reduction in histone H3 lysine 9 acetylation (H3K9ac). Loss of either ASF1 isoform reduced basal H3K9ac levels, whereas restoration of ASF1 counteracted the ICP22-associated reduction in H3K9ac, supporting a functional link between ASF1 and H3K9ac regulation. Integrated H3K9ac CUT&Tag and RNA sequencing further showed that the presence of ICP22 was associated with reduced H3K9ac occupancy and concordant transcriptional changes at host genomic loci. ICP22 expression also reduced the detectable association between ASF1 and histone H3 under the experimental conditions examined. Notably, complete loss of either ASF1 isoform impaired the replication of both wild-type and ICP22-deleted viruses, indicating that basal ASF1 function remains necessary for efficient HSV-1 replication. Together, these findings identify ASF1-associated H3K9ac regulation as a previously unrecognized component of ICP22-mediated host chromatin remodeling and reveal that HSV-1 modulates, rather than completely inactivates, an ASF1-dependent host function required for productive infection.

title: Iron affects association and dissociation rates of α-synuclein iron-responsive element mRNA binding to iron regulatory protein in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: The interaction of α-synuclein (α-Syn) mRNA with iron regulatory protein 1 (IRP1) may influence translation through an iron-responsive element (IRE) mRNA in the 5'-untranslated region (5'-UTR). We measured the kinetics of α-Syn RNA/IRP1 binding across RNA concentrations and temperatures, with and without Fe2+, and examined the interaction by molecular docking. In the absence of Fe2+, the observed binding rate constant (kobs) increased approximately linearly from 37 s-1 at 0.1 μM RNA to 358 s-1 at 1.0 μM RNA. Kinetic analysis yielded an association rate constant (kon) of 347 μM-1 s-1 and a dissociation rate constant (koff) of 11.6 s-1; addition of 50 μM Fe2+ reduced kon to 138 μM-1 s-1 and increased koff to 18 s-1. From 5 to 25 °C, kobs increased from 79 to 417 s-1 without Fe2+ and from 23 to 256 s-1 with Fe2+. Fe2+ also increased the estimated activation energy for binding from 10.5 to 20.4 kcal/mol. Molecular docking predicted hydrogen-bond-mediated contacts between α-Syn RNA and internal pockets of IRP1. Together, the measured decrease in association rate, increase in dissociation rate, and change in activation energy demonstrate that Fe2+ alters α-Syn RNA/IRP1 binding kinetics, providing an experimentally grounded mechanism to investigate iron-dependent regulation of α-Syn translation.

title: Regulatory roles and mechanistic insights of chromatin 3D structure in mammalian growth and development: A research progress review.
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) genome organization is closely linked to gene regulation and cell fate during mammalian development. This review examines how 3D chromatin architecture is established and dynamically remodeled from gametogenesis and early embryogenesis to postnatal development and disease. Rather than providing a conventional summary of hierarchical genome organization, we focus on the interplay among loop extrusion, biomolecular condensation, transcriptional and RNA-mediated regulation, and developmental context. Particular attention is given to species-associated differences in early embryonic genome reconstruction and to the unresolved relationship between chromatin architecture, transcriptional regulation, and developmental outcomes. We also discuss emerging technologies and their limitations in distinguishing structural associations from causal regulatory relationships.

title: mRNA folding facilitates efficient and spleen-targeted delivery by highly branched poly(β-amino ester)s.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutics hold great promise in preventing and treating various diseases. However, the instability and high immunogenicity of raw mRNA molecules, along with the inefficient delivery vectors, strictly limited the proteins translation and therapeutic applications. In this work, we successfully engineered a folded structural mRNA for enhancing its stability by leveraging a magnesium ion (Mg2+)-mediated charge neutralization and structural compression strategy. Further, a functionalized highly branched poly(β-amino ester)s (HPAEs) was utilized to efficiently deliver the folded mRNA, achieving specifically targeting to the spleen. Notably, compared with polyplexes containing non-folded mRNA, the optimal folded mRNA-based polyplexes exhibited stronger mRNA encapsulation, smaller size, and a more homogeneous morphology; ultimately, demonstrated higher mRNA transfection efficiency up to 85.4% across five different cell types, maintaining high cell viability. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that Mg2+-mediated mRNA folding strategy dramatically enhanced the folded mRNA-formulated polyplexes cellular uptake and endosomal escape. Encouragingly, when administered systemically, the representative folded mRNA-based polyplexes demonstrated robust protein expression, yielding 3-fold enhancement in spleen, compared to the unfolded mRNA-based nanoparticles, showing superior biosafety in vivo. Collectively, the work establishes a new class of the folded structure mRNA polymer delivery system, and provides a foundation for the next generation of RNA-based therapeutic drugs for spleen-related diseases.

title: Reduced BNIP1 impairs autophagosome-lysosome fusion in hippocampal neurons and contributes to Alzheimer's disease pathology.
abstract: BNIP1 (BCL2‑interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N‑ethylmaleimide‑sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting that BNIP1 is a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP‑overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells, screened key interacting proteins of BNIP1 via mass spectrometry, and further performed gain‑ and loss‑of‑function assays using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNA (siRNA) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that, in these experimental models, reduced BNIP1 expression contributes to AD‑related pathological alterations by impairing autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b‑mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. This study suggests that reduced BNIP1 expression is involved in AD‑related pathological alterations.NIP1 (BCL2-interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, which renders BNIP1 a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP-overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells. Mass-spectrometry analysis was performed to screen key interacting proteins of BNIP1. Gain- and loss-of-function experiments were further conducted using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that decreased BNIP1 may act as an important contributing factor mediating AD-associated autophagosome-lysosome fusion defects in these experimental models. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b-mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates aberrant autophagosome-lysosome fusion. This study suggests that BNIP1 serves as a potentially key regulatory protein for mechanistic research into Alzheimer's disease.

title: Clomipramine hydrochloride restricts feline infectious peritonitis virus replication in immortalized and primary feline cells.
abstract: Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP), caused by feline coronavirus (FCoV), is a severe and often fatal disease in cats. Although recent advances in antiviral therapy have improved clinical outcomes, limitations related to cost, accessibility, regulatory approval, and antiviral resistance highlight the need for additional therapeutic strategies. Host-directed antiviral approaches targeting cellular processes required for viral replication may represent an alternative strategy. In this study, we investigated whether clomipramine hydrochloride, a veterinary drug with lysosomotropic properties and previously reported antiviral activity against several enveloped viruses, could inhibit FIPV replication. Clomipramine pretreatment reduced FIPV RNA and protein expression and decreased infectious virus production in Crandell-Rees Feline Kidney (CRFK) cells in a concentration-dependent manner, with an EC50 of 10.8 μM. The calculated CC50 was 60.5 μM, corresponding to a selectivity index of 5.6. Clomipramine also retained antiviral activity when administered immediately after infection or at 4 h postinfection, although the effect was reduced with delayed treatment. Antiviral activity was further observed in primary feline cells derived from abdominal and pleural effusion samples. Clomipramine treatment reduced FIPV-induced expression of the interferon-stimulated genes MX1 and CXCL10, while clomipramine alone did not induce their expression in uninfected cells. The reduction in MX1 and CXCL10 expression closely paralleled the decrease in viral RNA levels, suggesting that these changes were likely associated with reduced viral stimulation rather than direct induction or suppression of these interferon-stimulated genes. LysoTracker staining showed reduced fluorescence in FIPV-infected cells, whereas staining was retained in clomipramine-treated infected cells. These findings may reflect reduced virus-associated perturbation of lysosomal compartments following inhibition of FIPV replication. Together, these findings identify clomipramine as a potential host-directed antiviral candidate against FIPV and support further investigation of its antiviral activity and therapeutic potential.

title: StWRKY40 and StMAPK3 positively regulate drought tolerance in potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) via mediating osmotic adjustment, photosynthetic capacity, and antioxidant defense.
abstract: Potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) is a vital global food crop whose yield is severely constrained by drought stress. Both WRKY transcription factors (TFs) and the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway have been established as key components of plant stress response networks. However, the specific molecular regulatory mechanisms by which they coordinately mediate drought tolerance in potato remain largely elusive. This study identified and functionally characterized how StWRKY40 and StMAPK3 cooperatively confer drought resistance, confirming their core regulatory roles in drought tolerance in potato. Phylogenetic analysis classified StWRKY40 into the WRKY Group II-a subfamily. Both StWRKY40 and StMAPK3 were strongly induced by drought stress. Protein-protein interaction assays confirmed a direct physical interaction between nucleus-localized StWRKY40 and StMAPK3, primarily in the nucleus. Transgenic potato lines overexpressing either StWRKY40 or StMAPK3 exhibited significantly enhanced drought tolerance. This was evidenced by improved growth metrics, enhanced photosynthetic capacity, and strengthened osmotic adjustment, with lower osmotic potentials of proline, soluble sugars, and proteins. Overexpression lines also exhibited upregulated expression of stress-responsive genes (StCAT, StPOD, StSOD, and StP5CS), elevated antioxidant enzyme activities (SOD, CAT, POD), and reduced levels of H2O2 and malondialdehyde (MDA). In contrast, RNA interference (RNAi) lines displayed pronounced drought-sensitive phenotypes relative to non-transgenic (NT) controls, showing opposite trends across all assessed parameters. This study elucidates the coordinate role of StWRKY40 and StMAPK3 as key regulators of drought resistance in potato, providing a theoretical foundation and valuable genetic resources for molecular breeding.

title: Immunization with JN.1 spike protein increases the breadth of binding and neutralizing antibodies in Syrian hamsters in an immune-history dependent manner.
abstract: With much of the world exposed to previous variants of SARS-CoV-2, testing of current COVID-19 vaccines in preclinical models should occur in the context of preexisting immunity to the virus. Here, we evaluated the immunogenicity and efficacy of a JN.1 variant spike (S) protein-based nanoparticle vaccine in Syrian hamsters nine months after three immunizations with Wuhan-1 prototype, prototype + BA.5, or XBB.1.5 variant COVID-19 vaccines. Serum was collected prior to and three weeks after the JN.1 immunization to measure antibody responses to different variants of SARS-CoV-2, including JN.1 and KP.2. To assess efficacy, age-matched naive and JN.1 vaccine-boosted hamsters were challenged with the KP.2 variant of SARS-CoV-2, and viral burden in the nasal turbinates, trachea, and lungs was measured. Three doses of the nanoparticle S protein vaccine induced long-lasting virus neutralizing antibody responses, and neutralization of the JN.1 and KP.2 variants of SARS-CoV-2 was associated with one or more doses of the XBB.1.5 vaccine. Subsequent immunization with the JN.1 variant vaccine boosted JN.1 and KP.2 specific antibody responses, however, the relative increase in titer was dependent on vaccine history and inversely correlated with JN.1 neutralizing titers prior to boosting. Following challenge, JN.1-boosted hamsters, regardless of their immune history or increase in JN.1 specific antibody response, were protected against the KP.2 variant with infectious virus titers averaging at or below the limit of detection in all tissues. The reductions in viral RNA levels correlated with pre-challenge serum antibody titers against KP.2. In conclusion, boosting with a variant SARS-CoV-2 vaccine is effective in a diverse immune landscape and protects against a related virus variant.

title: Integrator complex removes lesion-stalled RNA polymerase II after transcription-coupled repair to facilitate transcription restart.
abstract: Gene transcription by RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) is highly vulnerable to transcription-blocking DNA lesions (TBLs), which, if unresolved, induce transcription stress leading to cellular decline and aging. TBLs are removed by transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (TC-NER). TC-NER is initiated when Cockayne syndrome group B protein recognizes lesion-stalled Pol II and promotes TC-NER complex assembly. This complex recruits TFIIH for lesion verification, followed by incision and repair to enable transcription restart. Many TBLs stall Pol II within its active site, shielding the lesion from repair and requiring Pol II processing to expose it. However, whether this occurs through Pol II backtracking or release from the DNA, and the regulatory mechanisms involved, remain poorly defined. Here, we identified the Integrator complex as a key factor in lesion-stalled Pol II processing. Interaction proteomics revealed Integrator recruitment to late-stage TC-NER complexes. Integrator's endonuclease core promotes efficient transcription recovery after TBL induction, without affecting lesion removal by TC-NER. Live-cell imaging and chromatin retention assays demonstrated that Integrator facilitates Pol II release from DNA following TC-NER. Collectively, these findings support a two-step mechanism for Pol II clearance during TC-NER, wherein TFIIH-mediated backtracking exposes the lesion for repair, followed by Integrator-mediated Pol II release to restore transcription.

title: Hantaviral therapeutics: life cycle targets and chemotherapeutic interventions.
abstract: Orthohantaviruses represent a persistent global health threat, being responsible for life-threatening diseases such as Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS). Despite high case fatality rates and recent outbreaks, there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines. Clinical management remains heavily reliant on supportive care and repurposed drugs, which often exhibit limited efficacy and dose-limiting toxicities. This review examines rational drug design strategies targeting critical steps in the viral life cycle, specifically Gn/Gc-mediated cellular entry and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)-driven genome replication. We evaluate the current landscape of viral inhibitors, including peptidomimetics, nucleoside analogues, and naturally derived compounds. To accelerate the discovery of novel treatments, we advocate for the integration of modern in silico screening to evaluate extensive chemical and natural product libraries. These broad compound collections offer a structurally diverse and largely untapped reservoir for antiviral development. Ultimately, expanding preclinical testing to include globally neglected variants will be essential to develop broad-spectrum hantaviral therapeutics capable of mitigating future epidemic threats.

title: Divergent dependence on host gene sigma-1 receptor shapes hepatitis C and orthoflavivirus infection.
abstract: The Flaviviridae family encompasses major human pathogens, such as hepatitis C virus (HCV) and dengue virus (DENV). Despite shared genome organization and replication strategies, these viruses differ in host interactions, tissue tropism and replication dynamics, leading to distinct disease outcomes. Sigma-1 receptor (SIGMAR1) encodes an endoplasmic reticulum-associated protein that regulates lipid transport, autophagy and proteostasis. We previously showed that SIGMAR1 silencing reduces early HCV infection efficiency without affecting unrelated viruses. Here, we demonstrate that SIGMAR1 is rate-limiting for the formation of normal double-membrane vesicles (DMVs), the putative HCV replication compartments. In contrast, DENV and West Nile virus (WNV) RNA replication remained efficient following SIGMAR1 depletion, indicating a selective requirement for SIGMAR1 in HCV DMV formation. Notably, SIGMAR1 knockdown markedly impaired secretion of infectious DENV and WNV particles without reducing intracellular progeny, suggesting a role for SIGMAR1 in orthoflavivirus virion release. SIGMAR1 silencing also disrupted Golgi architecture and altered cellular detergent-resistant membrane composition, consistent with defects in vesicular trafficking. These findings identify SIGMAR1 as a host factor with distinct functions in the replication cycles of hepaciviruses and orthoflaviviruses and highlight its broader role in maintaining membrane organization required for efficient infection by Flaviviridae.

title: TARBP2 facilitates renal cell carcinoma immune escape by suppressing 53BP1 phase separation to upregulate B7-H3.
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) harbors an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment that facilitates immune evasion and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). However, the factors driving immune escape in RCC remain incompletely understood. In this study, transactivation response RNA-binding protein 2 (TARBP2) was identified as a critical regulator of the immune checkpoint molecule B7-H3. Elevated TARBP2 expression was associated with poor prognosis and ICB resistance in patients with RCC. Functionally, TARBP2 in RCC cells suppressed the intratumoral accumulation and cytotoxicity of T cells, particularly NK cells, thereby promoting immune escape. Mechanistically, nuclear TARBP2 interacted with p53-binding protein 1 (53BP1), inhibiting 53BP1 phase separation and subsequent p53 activation, thereby augmenting B7-H3 transcription. Furthermore, TARBP2 inhibition significantly enhanced ICB efficacy when combined with adoptive NK cell therapy. Collectively, these findings establish TARBP2 as a key mediator of immune evasion in RCC and a promising therapeutic target for overcoming ICB resistance.

title: M6A-modified Gata1 promotes endoplasmic reticulum stress during acute kidney injury via suppressing Sesn2 : Gata1 promotes acute kidney injury by downregulating Sesn2.
abstract: Renal ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) is a leading cause of acute kidney injury (AKI), which is closely related to endoplasmic reticulum stress (ERS). Gata binding protein 1 (Gata1) has been reported to be involved in ERS, but its role in renal tubular epithelial cell ERS under AKI conditions remains elusive. In this study, renal I/R-induced mouse model and hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R)-induced TCMK-1 cell model were established. Renal function and histomorphology were determined based on serum Scr and BUN level test and H&E staining, respectively. Cell function was tested by CCK-8 and TUNEL assays. Molecular mechanism was explored using luciferase reporter, chromatin immunoprecipitation, co-immunoprecipitation, and RNA immunoprecipitation assays. The results demonstrated that Gata1 was elevated in kidney tubular epithelial cells of I/R-induced mice and H/R-treated TCMK-1 cells (P < 0.001). Gata1 knockdown exerted protective effects against AKI, as manifested by improved renal pathological changes and inhibited ERS. Mechanistically, Gata1 inhibited the transcription of Sestrin2 (Sesn2) via recruiting histone deacetylase 2 (Hdac2) in TCMK-1 cells. Moreover, Gata1 knockdown upregulated Sesn2 expression, thus mitigating ERS in H/R-stimulated TCMK-1 cells. As for the upstream molecular mechanism, Gata1 mRNA was stabilized through N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification mediated by methyltransferase-like14 (Mettl14)/insulin-like growth factor-2 mRNA-binding protein 2 (Igf2bp2). Furthermore, Mettl14 knockdown inhibited ERS by downregulating Gata1. In conclusion, Mettl14/Igf2bp2-mediated m6A modification upregulated Gata1, which recruited Hdac2 to transcriptionally suppress Sesn2, thus exacerbating ERS and AKI.

title: CircCCNB1 Inhibits Ferroptosis in Glioblastoma Cells via the USP4/IGF2BP1/SLC7A11 Axis.
abstract: Characterized by high heterogeneity, invasive growth and malignant astrocytic features, glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary tumor of the central nervous system and a leading cause of neurological tumor-related morbidity and mortality worldwide. This study is supposed to explore the potential role and mechanism of CirCCCNB1 on ferroptosis in GBM cells, contributing theoretical advancements for the treatment of GBM. RNA levels and protein expression were detected by qRT-PCR and WB. Cell proliferation, MDA, GSH, ROS and Fe2+ contents were determined by CCK-8 and kits. RNA pull-down, RIP, Co-IP and MeRIP were performed. Finally, overexpression of IGF2BP1, USP4 or SLC7A11 was combined with sh-CircCCNB1 to verify the mechanism. Results showed that CircCCNB1 was overexpressed in GBM cells. Downregulation of CircCCNB1 promoted GBM cell ferroptosis. CircCCNB1 acts as a molecular scaffold to form a functional ternary complex between USP4 and IGF2BP1, and USP4 deubiquitinates and stabilizes IGF2BP1 through deubiquitinase activity. Moreover, IGF2BP1 recognized and bound to the m6A site on SLC7A11 mRNA and enhanced SLC7A11 stability. Rescue experiment confirmed that overexpression of IGF2BP1, USP4 or SLC7A11 could partially rescue the promotive effect of CircCCNB1 knockdown on ferroptosis in GBM cells. In conclusion, CircCCNB1 recruits USP4 and IGF2BP1 for ternary‑complex formation, stabilizes IGF2BP1, enhances the stability of SLC7A11 mRNA, thus suppressing ferroptosis in GBM cells.

title: Association of tonsillar Pseudomonas identified by 16S rRNA sequencing with clinical remission after tonsillectomy in IgA nephropathy: a machine learning approach.
abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that mucosal immune responses in the tonsils may be associated with clinical features of immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN). This study characterised the tonsillar microbiota implicated in IgAN using 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing. We retrospectively analysed tonsillar tissues from 20 patients with biopsy-proven IgAN and 19 patients with recurrent tonsillitis (RT) who underwent tonsillectomy. The microbiota composition was determined via 16S rRNA sequencing, and the disease-associated genera were identified using the Boruta feature selection algorithm. Their associations with clinical outcomes after tonsillectomy were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, Kaplan-Meier analysis, and log-rank tests. A total of 194 and 190 genera were detected for IgAN and RT. The α-diversity did not differ significantly between the groups, but the β-diversity analysis revealed distinct microbial community structures (p < 0.01). Boruta identified Actinomyces, Parvimonas, Streptococcus, Catonella, Bacillus, and Pseudomonas as key discriminating genera. Pseudomonas and Bacillus were enriched in the IgAN group. The area under the curve for the prediction of complete remission at 3 years based on Pseudomonas abundance was 0.712. The complete remission and proteinuria remission rates were significantly higher for the patients with Pseudomonas (p = 0.03 for both). This study reveals distinct tonsillar microbiota profiles between patients with IgAN and those with RT and shows that tonsillar Pseudomonas enrichment was associated with favourable outcomes after tonsillectomy. These findings suggest that tonsillar Pseudomonas may be associated with clinical remission after tonsillectomy in IgAN.

title: Feature Selection and Machine Learning Strategies to Develop a Minimal Bioassay for Cholangiocarcinoma Subtype.
abstract: To demonstrate that the combination of feature selection and machine learning methods can curate affordable, accurate RNA sequencing-based assays for cholangiocarcinoma subtype that achieve comparable results to expensive, time-intensive multiomic analysis. From 43 cholangiocarcinomas treated at Mayo Clinic in Minnesota (May 1, 1996, to July 30, 2019) and 206 treated at Fudan University in China (2009 to 2015), 35,449 RNA, protein, and phosphoprotein features were extracted. These multiomic features were used to assign patients to 3 molecular classes. Important RNA sequencing features were selected by competing feature selection methods. Machine learning classification models were tested on each feature set. Accuracy, F1 score, area under the curve, precision, and recall were validated for each feature selection and predictive model combination, bootstrapping using up-sampled, class-balanced data.
